extracted.intended_audience: student journalists, reporters, and editors (journalism students)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for writing clear, forceful newspaper copy and editorials — including voice for radio announcers, classification and structure of editorials, and five concrete elements of newspaper English (wording, nouns, verbs, concision, simplicity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Announcers' responsibility in spoken English
rubrics_metrics.description: Announcers, who are heard daily by millions, have a special responsibility as examples in pronunciation, enunciation and vocal diction generally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Announcers' authoritative pronunciation and diction will have a tremendous influence on listeners; they should aim to approximate a high standard of English to improve American speech. Anti-pattern: casual or slovenly pronunciation that misleads or degrades public speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radio speakers and public addresses should model good English
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who make addresses or give short talks on the radio should be examples in the use of good English; many speakers prepare and thus have better-than-average speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speakers should prepare their addresses, cultivate clear utterance, and avoid sloppy or unprepared speech. The page notes many cultured speakers provide essentials and refinements of utterance for listeners to learn from.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial purpose classification (explain / interpret / comment / argue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorials should be analyzed and written according to their primary purpose: to explain, interpret, comment, or argue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or composing an editorial, identify which purpose it serves (explanatory, interpretive, commentary, or argumentative). Exercises ask students to classify editorials on this basis and to note the tone appropriate to each purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial structure — the three parts of an editorial
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorials possess three parts (exercise: 'Analyze for the three parts of an editorial').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text directs students to clip editorials and 'analyze for the three parts of an editorial' (implying a recognizable structure to be learned and applied). While labels for the three parts are not given on this page, the pedagogy expects identification of those parts and notes method used in each development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of the opening sentence of an editorial
rubrics_metrics.description: The opening sentence of an editorial is significant and can be used as the springboard for the piece (exercise: underline the opening sentence and write from it an account that might have stimulated the editorial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice: identify and reuse the opening sentence to reconstruct the stimulus or background for the editorial — implying the opening should clearly connect to the issue or provoke the argument/explanation that follows. Anti-pattern: an obscure or irrelevant opening that fails to orient the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short words, short sentences, short paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Use short Anglo‑Saxon words where possible; prefer short sentences and short paragraphs for clarity and to aid rapid reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short words carry force; choose the short word where there is a choice. Short sentences prevent readers from getting lost in complex clauses — even a choppy style is preferable to convoluted smoothness that hides meaning. Newspaper paragraphs are units of type and should be short to assist the eye; a column of unbroken type is monotonous. Examples: compare number of polysyllabic words in poems and news copy; prefer concise phrasing. Anti-pattern: long, intricate sentences and long paragraphs that impede quick comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the concrete noun (the particular, the specific)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer the concrete, particular, and specific noun to vague, abstract, or general terms so the reader gets a definite picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example contrast: 'The Marmon purred down Fifth Avenue' is superior to 'The car came softly down the street.' The precise word prevents multiple mental images and makes reporting accurate. The page gives tests and literary examples to show how concreteness clarifies meaning. Anti-pattern: vague terms like 'car' or 'street' that leave readers guessing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the live (active) verb
rubrics_metrics.description: Use active verbs rather than passive constructions; the live verb makes narrative move and reportage objective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid passive circumlocutions such as 'he was given an Arista pin' or 'The moon was seen riding the clouds.' Instead, use active constructions: 'The moon rode the clouds.' Reporters should record what they saw directly. Anti-pattern: overuse of passive voice and circumlocutory phrasing that slows action and obscures agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness — every inch of space counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Be concise by consciously selecting concrete nouns and live verbs; brevity is a virtue because newspaper space is limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conciseness follows from precise nouns and active verbs and avoids unnecessary words, phrases, and clauses. The paper should 'sparkle with as much news as its columns will hold.' Anti-pattern: burying news under unnecessary verbiage; wasting column inches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Straightforwardness and simplicity (write so all readers understand)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write directly and simply — ask how you'd tell the neighbor (Bill Jones) — so the reader has no doubt; simplicity and straightforwardness support clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the writer becomes involved in complex thought, pause and restate simply. Use vivid comparisons to elucidate vague terms (e.g., 'not much larger than a rat-hole') so meaning is unmistakable. Study parables and poetry to learn particularity and striking comparison. Anti-pattern: ornate, indirect prose that requires the reader to infer basic meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid jargon; make copy understandable to readers of varied vocabularies
rubrics_metrics.description: Good journalism requires language that 'all readers, whether of wide or meager vocabulary, may understand' — avoid jargon and unnecessarily long or technical words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter title 'NEWSPAPER ENGLISH VS. JARGON' and references to recommended readings on 'Jargon' indicate a standard: prefer plain language and explain or replace technical terms with familiar comparisons. Anti-pattern: using specialized or long words that alienate or confuse average readers.
